newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain raises interest rate to 6.25 percent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain raises interest rate to 6.25 percent.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Tuesday raised official interest rates to 6.25 percent from six percent, just four days after taking power, and gave the central bank greater powers in a radical move that changes the mechanics of setting monetary policy.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown brought forward a planned meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George by 24 hours and told reporters afterwards he was giving the central bank independence to set interest rates.

Until now the finance minister has set rates after taking advice from the Bank of England. Former finance minister Kenneth Clarke had ignored George's advice for an interest rate rise for some months before the May 1 election.

The economy has been growing at more than three percent and George was concerned about the build-up of inflationary pressures. Brown said the Treasury will continue to set the inflation target, which will remain at 2.5 percent.
Brown said this target would have been overshot without higher rates.
"My judgement is that we have inherited a situation in which, in the absence of corrective action, inflation will overshoot the government's inflation target next year," he said.
Citibank and Barclays, one of Britain's big four banks, said they would mirror the rise in official rates and raise their base lending rates to 6.25 percent.
Government bonds rose sharply after Brown's announcement. Sterling also jumped after initially dipping on the news.
Brown said his government would aim to break the boom-bust cycles that hobbled British economic performance for decades.
"The enemy of growth and the investment necessary for it is the instability of short periodic bursts of high growth followed by recession," Brown said.
"We must break from the short-termism of the past and the economic instability that has characterised the British economy, not just in recent years but for most of the century."

Brown said the government will give the Bank of England its own exchange reserves to help steer policy and a new "monetary policy committee", meeting every month, would have nine members -- including an extra deputy governor and four members from outside the bank.
Giving the Bank of England full independence would be one step towards helping Britian fulfil conditions for signing up to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
However, Brown told the news conference it was unlikely that Britain would be an EMU member in the first wave due to start in 1999.
In response to Brown's moves, the Bank of England said it believes Brown's proposals on the bank's status would help ensure inflation objectives were met.

Under Brown's proposals the inflation target will be confirmed in each budget statement and the Bank will still be required to publish a quarterly inflation report to justify its monetary operations and its analysis of the economy.
It will also have to explain how it intends to meet the inflation target, the Treasury said.

The legislation will provide that if "in extreme economic circumstances, the national interest demands it, the government will have the power to give instructions to the Bank on interest rates for a limited period," Brown said.
"This power is in line with practice in other countries and could only be exercised through...legislation approved by parliament," Brown said.
